title: Exercise 7B · Q15
summary: Compare the areas of a square, a circle and an equilateral triangle, all with the same perimeter.
alt: A designer makes tabletops of the same perimeter, 132 cm, as a square, a circle and an equilateral triangle, and compares their areas.

steps.title: The question
steps.narration: A designer makes three children's tabletops — a **square**, a **circle** and an **equilateral triangle** — each with the same **perimeter, 132 cm**. (Take π = 22/7.) We compare their areas to see which shape gives the most tabletop for the same amount of edging.

steps.title: (a)(i) Side of the square
steps.narration: A square has **4 equal sides**, so divide the perimeter by 4.\[\begin{aligned}\role{sq}{\text{side}} &= 132 \div 4 = \role{ans}{33\ \text{cm}}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: (b) Areas of the square and circle
steps.narration: Square: **side²**. Circle: **πr²**.\[\begin{aligned}\text{Area of square} &= 33^2 = \role{ans}{1089\ \text{cm}^2}\\ \text{Area of circle} &= \tfrac{22}{7}\times 21^2 = \tfrac{22}{7}\times 441 = \role{ans}{1386\ \text{cm}^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: (c)(ii) Area of the equilateral triangle
steps.narration: An equilateral triangle of side **s** has area **(√3/4)s²**.\[\begin{aligned}\text{Area} &= \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\times 44^2 = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\times 1936 = 484\sqrt3 = \role{ans}{838\ \text{cm}^2}\ \text{(3 s.f.)}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: (d) Which shape wins?
steps.narration: Compare the three areas for the **same perimeter** of 132 cm.\[\begin{aligned}\role{ci}{\text{circle}}&: 1386\ \text{cm}^2 \;>\; \role{sq}{\text{square}}: 1089\ \text{cm}^2 \;>\; \role{tr}{\text{triangle}}: 838\ \text{cm}^2\end{aligned}\]The designer should choose the **circular (round)** tabletop — it gives the **greatest area** for the same perimeter.

formulas.title: Perimeter → side/radius
formulas.text: Divide the perimeter by the number of equal sides (square, triangle); for a circle, solve the circumference formula for r.

formulas.title: Areas
formulas.text: Three different area formulas for the same perimeter.

challenges.title: Greatest area?
challenges.prompt: For the same perimeter, which of the three shapes has the greatest area?
challenges.explain: The circle's 1386 cm² beats the square's 1089 cm² and the triangle's 838 cm² — for a fixed perimeter, a circle always encloses the most area.

takeaways: For a **fixed perimeter**, different shapes enclose very different **areas**.
Among simple shapes, a **circle** always gives the greatest area for a given perimeter — and a shape with more sides beats one with fewer.
This question uses **perimeter and area formulas**, not Pythagoras' theorem — not every real-world question in this exercise needs a right-angled triangle.

notes.title: Why no Pythagoras here?
notes.text: This question is about **perimeter and area**, a different (but related) topic. It is included in Exercise 7B because real-world problem-solving often mixes several kinds of formulas.
